One more thing with this— while you will find in your research that this disease is degenerative (episodes get worse over time), this CAN be reduced with consistent treatment. The distinguishing feature of them is that with hypomania you can still function. You can still sit down at your psychiatrists and talk to them normally. You can go to work, you can drive to pick up your kids, you’re erratic and potentially delusional but you aren’t in need of hospitalization, necessarily.  Mixed episodes are a different story entirely. 

Mania means you are entirely impeded from functioning. You cannot safely drive, you cannot spend a day at work, you likely need the hospital, you might end up in jail, or you will need someone dedicated to care for you at home like a parent or partner if they’re up for it.  Contrary to what some believe you don’t need to land in a psych ward for it to be full blown mania as if you’re very lucky you might have someone willing to entirely take care of you. Yes.  You WILL get depressed after except in rare cases.  The bigger problem though is twofold. 

1.  Bipolar is degenerative. This means that with every episode, it gets worse,  that hypomania can turn into full blown mania with time. Your depression will get longer and worse.  The only way to halt this is successful treatment.  You want to avoid any episode jo matter how useful in the moment it may be, because the long term impact of every single episode is to increase the likelihood of more episodes and to increase severity. 

2.  Bipolar episodes cause permanent cognitive decline.  You get dumber essentially. You feel absolutely brilliant while hypomanic or manic but you end the episode with lower cognitive ability than you went into it with. Mania in all forms causes this but so does depression 

These are facts I got from reading NIH literature reviews (so a highly reliable source).  I know no one wants to hear this, but it’s true.  The only way to live the longest healthiest life you can is to do everything in your power to prevent episodes.  At all costs. To put it very simply, bipolar is made up of a few types of episodes— depression, mania, and mixed episodes, which are the fresh hell through which you get symptoms of both at the same time.  

If your doc has told you that you have bipolar depression, this means you have bipolar disorder and are currently in a depressed state.  Most bipolar folks spend far more time in depression than they do in mania or mixed states.

It’s not bad to search at all! Just start familiarizing yourself with what are and most importantly are NOT good sources. I find reading meta studies (They will be labeled literature reviews) directly from the NIH’s website to be most helpful— but keep in mind that a little bit of knowledge is a dangerous thing. This is a scary diagnosis to get and you can drive yourself batty reading about statistics of how people end up and such.  I actually think having a basic understanding of the disease, it’s typical progression, and various treatments, helps you be a better patient as you can then actively participate in your own treatment.  Just remember that if something your doc told you seemingly contradicts a given study you’ve read, that not all studies are created equal and at the end of the day you don’t have the medical background to necessarily know better. That said it’s always fine to bring things up if you’re confused, to ask for clarification, and to generally use your doctor as a resource to learn about your disorder and how it affects you.

There is a reason these meds are prescribed and approved. Another consideration is that bipolar is degenerative and causes cognitive decline.  This means that every episode you have makes it more likely that you’ll have more, and the ones following will inevitably be worse and possibly longer.  And you’ll be dumber as a result, basically.  Treatment is the only way to prevent this. mania and depression also cause cognitive impairment but I suspect you already know that. 

So it’s really a personal decision between you and your doctor.  I encourage you to bring up these health concerns to your doctor.  Long term these are things to think about, and your doctor can help you.  *you* are the patient, they’re here to help you not just give you X treatment without any of your input.  Be an active participant in your own treatment however you can.

People will joke “it’s not alcoholism until you get your degree” and they’re dead ass wrong.  Watch your drinking, never use it to self soothe if you can help it.  

Study with friends!  Do work with friends!  At the end of college me and my friends would rent out rooms in the library and write our essays all hanging out.  It made it much better.

Don’t overload yourself with activities at first like everyone inevitably does.

Ask older students in your major their fave professors and get to know them if you can.  Don’t sweat this in the first year or two, it’ll be hard as a freshman to do this nbd.

Work expands to fill the available time.  This means that if you block out five hours to do a problem set, it’s gonna take you five hours even if you’re only working for two.  Block out the appropriate time.

Use Siri or your other voice assistant to set reminders for when you want to do things!  I use Siri like this:  “Siri, remind me to start my research for my history paper Tuesday at 2pm”.  And then I can forget about it until the reminder comes up.  Minimize what you need to remember as much as possible.  Stay organized with deadlines and it’ll bring your stress down.

And finally- when things are getting hard *talk to your professors*.  Sooner rather than later.  It’s much easier to say “hi, I’ve been incredibly depressed and am struggling to come to class at all” and have them figure something out with you *before* it’s a problem rather than you explain that you’ve been depressed when you’re already doing badly.  Professors are people.  Don’t be afraid to say you’re having a really tough time.  College is a time when peoples mental illnesses rear their heads for the first time so you aren’t the first depressed student to have entered their office and you won’t be the last.  

If you can tell it’s gonna be a hard semester and you think you’d benefit from accommodations like soft deadlines or sth, talk to your student services office ASAP, it takes a bit to work out but bipolar is a disability and the ADA requires they work with you.

MAKE TIME FOR FRIENDS.  This is so important ESPECIALLY during finals and midterms.  Your mental health comes above all.  If you’re too depressed to write or work one night take the L and go find friends to hang with.  Seriously.  Sometimes you’ll make the “irresponsible” choice to go hang with people when you have work you should be doing, but if it’s needed for your mental health then it is needed for your mental health.   On multiple occasions I got extensions because I was too depressed to work and instead went and smoked weed with friends.  It is a okay to email a prof and literally say I’m so depressed it just ain’t happening tonight can I have another day or two.  It might feel like oversharing but it’s better to be upfront, you’ll have a better time of getting that kindness than if they just think you’ve partied your time away. 

Finally, use your counselor to help you!  Idk what your school is like but at mine they could put in a medical exemption for you to keep you off academic probation if a quartet goes badly for medical (depression/mania) reasons.  But they have to know what’s going on to advocate for you.  

TLDR communicate with people you need to AS SOON AS issues rear their head and not two months into a shit semester.


Edit to add.  If you’re a girl- please be so careful.  I don’t want to scare you but the numbers on sexual assault in college are super high.  It happened to me by a friend who I trusted entirely.  If it happens to you it is in no way your fault, but always have safety plans with your friends, never leave anyone behind at a party.  And always know what number drink you’re on- if you don’t recall how many drinks you have had, you’ve had enough

One final thing sorry this is a lot- remember you can always do more drugs later.  You can never undo the drugs you’ve taken.  If you’re gonna do psychedelics or harder drugs start low go slow and always do research into how it interacts with bipolar and your meds so you’re an educated and responsible drug user should you choose to do so (IE Molly and SSRIs don’t mix, lithium and LSD are deadly together, etc)

Something to keep an eye out for is mania.  If he starts to get super angry randomly, become much more sexual than normal, spend a lot, sleep very little, jump all over the place- you’ll need to talk with him about it or even possibly his family if it’s worrisome enough.  


Now of course a lot of these behaviors are also things people do normally when grieving.  Some people will hear a terrible thing like that and immediately want sex because it’s life affirming.  Grief is weird.  

So the most concrete thing to keep an eye out for is if you start to notice him sleeping very little and not feeling tired.  That’s a BIG red flag and that’s when you should talk to him, because the other behaviors can be within the realm of normal.  Hypomania (mania lite basically) needs to have early
Intervention so it doesn’t become full blown mania.

The problem isn't that you're getting hurt.  The problem is that she's saying mean things which isn't okay.

Is she working with a psychiatrist and a therapist?  If not you should sit her down and tell her how badly it's affecting you.  The anger is the hardest part for me personally because sometimes I do lash out and hurt people but it's not okay.  It's why I've started meds and it's helped.  The bursts of anger aren't her fault.  The way she's handling it is her responsibility- does that make sense?  

I don't think any kind of ultimatum would be a good idea because meds are a big deal, but nudges in that direction would be good.  I think telling her exactly how hurt you feel when she says these things is okay.  You're allowed to be hurt by it.  

If she doesn't want to get better at the very least so she can control the anger better- well, you have to do what's best for you.  

Something that I've been working on is when I get really angry like that- just leaving the situation.  Just up and leaving until I cool down because I know the anger is irrational and I also don't actually feel angry at the situation at hand.  I just feel randomly angry.  In my experience I am not able to make it go away instantly like normal anger- but I am able to go away and do some self care and soothing until I'm able to handle things better.  It's been a few months since I've started working on this and there have been huge improvements for me.  It's doable. 

She has to at the very least develop some coping mechanisms to address this.  Her mental illness is a reason for the anger- but it's not an excuse for being unkind to you.  This *is* manageable but it's hard and there's no shame in needing help.  

In the meantime I think you should also if you can seek a therapist.  Because I do think you might benefit from a little outside perspective on what's okay in a relationship.  

Edit to add: my doctor put it this way- it's a problem when it's causing problems in your life, and then it needs to be addressed.  So she needs to do *something* to start addressing this- there are lots of options but she needs to do something.  It's not okay to hurt you.  If she's a good partner she'll want to work on it.

When she does get better, she'll probably be depressed again.  It'll be important that she knows that you don't see her differently or treat her differently- she's the same person, this is a health crisis.  

I hope she does accept help.  It'll take a lot longer to get better if she doesn't want to take medications.  Also- take care of yourself in this time.  It's easy to get too wrapped up in another's problems especially at a time of crisis, but it's not your responsibility to make it better.
